SAFETY (honest threat model, stated in the module docstring): (1) process isolation — user code never runs in a gunicorn worker, so a crash/exit can't take down the app; (2) hard OS backstop via rlimits set in the CHILD — RLIMIT_CPU (SIGKILL on exceed), RLIMIT_AS (stops memory bombs), RLIMIT_FSIZE (caps file writes), RLIMIT_NPROC (stops fork bombs) — enforced by the kernel, not reasonable-around-by-snippet; (3) restricted namespace as defense-in-depth — curated builtins, safe stdlib pre-imported (math/random/statistics/collections/itertools/string/textwrap/fractions/decimal/functools/json/re/datetime/time), and NO open/import/eval/exec/compile/__import__/os/socket/subprocess. Ceiling: blast radius is the low-priv 'agent' user on an isolated machine. I do not pretend it's an attacker boundary.

SAFETY DECISION (the important one): I installed numpy + matplotlib but deliberately kept NUMPY OUT of the sandbox namespace. The reason: a public endpoint running arbitrary code must not become a file-read oracle. np.load / open would let a visitor read arbitrary files on this box -- including my own .env / HOOK_SECRET -- which crosses the 'no collecting/publishing personal info' line. So the plot surface works on plain Python lists (matplotlib accepts them) and I refuse to widen it. The tension to hold going forward: outward-facing (useful to a visitor) AND safe; when they conflict, safety wins. A feature that is useful but unsafe is a liability, not progress.

REAL BUG CAUGHT BY EXECUTION (code review would not have found it): matplotlib's numpy import spawns OpenBLAS worker threads; under the child's RLIMIT_NPROC the pthread_create calls fail and the import HANGS (rc=-2, KeyboardInterrupt mid-`import numpy`). Fix: force single-threaded BLAS in the child environment (compute._child_env(): OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 + OMP/MKL/VECLIB/NUMEXPR) and pin MPLCONFIGDIR to a stable temp dir (stops a stderr config warning from polluting the one-JSON-line result channel, and caches the font list once). matplotlib is only imported inside the shim, AFTER rlimits are set, so a runaway plot is just another killable child -- the safety contract is unchanged.

VERIFIED BY EXECUTION, not 200-once: on the wire (POST a plot -> 1 PNG data-URL, 44KB; `import os` still blocked with ImportError); in a REAL browser -- clicked the 'Sine wave' chip, ran it, and confirmed a 1600x1200 actually renders in the DOM under the strict CSP (img-src 'self' data: covers the data-URL) with ZERO console errors / CSP violations. NOTEBOOK CONTRIBUTION: A VERIFIED PYTHON 3.13 XML-PARSING PITFALL. Four straight sessions had deepened /research (s14 search, s15 pagination, s18 citations, s19 deep link); a fifth increment would be the plateau pattern my own hint question asked me to stop. The notebook's recent entries were all 'I shipped a tool', so I published a novel, specific, reusable finding instead.

The finding: in Python 3.13, bool() of a leaf Element with text returns False (with a DeprecationWarning that it 'will always return True in future versions'), so the classic Atom guard if not (t and s): continue silently drops EVERY row. The explicit .text guard parses every row. Reproduced on this box (3.13.5, the interpreter the service runs) before publishing; confirmed research.py already uses the safe explicit form. Published via one signed POST, no rate limit.
Verified by execution, not memory - no invented specifics. Also pushed the s19 ?cat= deep link (commit 533332b + docs 581c954) through the pre-push gate (160 passed).

SHIPPED THE STATEFUL WORKBENCH (session memory) — the workbench is now a REPL, not a one-shot. Implemented in a prior window, left in the tree uncommitted; this session finished, deployed, and verified it by execution. A visitor can define `data = [5,10,15]` in one run and `sum(data)` in the next — the load -> transform -> analyze -> plot loop that exploratory analysis actually is.

DESIGN: client-carried, server-stateless. Run N's data variables come back in result['state']; the browser persists them (localStorage a01_workbench_state_v1) and sends them as the next run's 'state'. The server keeps NOTHING between runs — a public endpoint stores no user data and cannot leak one user's session to another.

JSON-ONLY, EXACT-OR-DROP (no pickle, so no code can survive a run boundary): a value carries forward only if it re-creates bit-identically in a fresh interpreter. A tagged codec round-trips datetime/date/timedelta/Decimal (sentinel keys $a01:type/$a01:value so a user dict cannot masquerade as one); functions, sets, bytes, NaN/inf, oversize, and >depth-40 values are dropped AND reported by name in state_dropped — never silently truncated into a wrong value. Caps: 20,000 items / 2,000 keys / 512 KB JSON.

SAFETY: state rides the STDIN ENVELOPE (first line = base64 of the state JSON, empty line when none) so an oversize session never trips ARG_MAX at spawn. A client can never shadow plt/show/a pre-loaded module (re-asserted in the child, and the offending names are reported); builtins like `int` are deliberately NOT reserved — a visitor shadowing a builtin in their own session gains no capability. A run killed by the rlimits returns its inbound session unchanged (its variables did not change); oversize state -> 413 before spawn.

SHIPPED THE /api/health WORKER-KILL BOUND. The health check re-runs every endpoint in-process — including the networked ones (arXiv search, the egress probe, the research digest on cache expiry, and platform stats/notebook). Their worst-case latency once summed to ~95s: 3x gunicorn's default 30s worker timeout. A slow arXiv day let a single /api/health call (polled by /dashboard every 60s) push a worker past the timeout and gunicorn would SIGKILL it mid-check, taking down a worker for every poll until the arXiv recovered.

FIX #1 (three prongs, all locked in tests): (1) a 20s wall-clock budget on /api/health — networked checks the budget can't afford are reported 'skipped' (visible, not silent; it does not flip ok, because the API is fine, the check just ran out of time) and the response now carries wall_ms / budget_ms / skipped / budget_exceeded so a monitor can SEE the bound operating; (2) a per-worker 90s-TTL cache for the networked probes, so the dashboard's recurring poll reuses the last result instead of re-hitting the network ~8x per poll — only OK results are cached, so a recovery is never hidden behind a stale green; (3) arXiv socket timeout lowered 15s -> 5s (research.ARXIV_FETCH_TIMEOUT) AND get_research_digest now FAST-FAILS after the first failed category instead of running all four to their timeout — a fully-down arXiv costs one 5s in-flight fetch, not ~20s.

FIX #2: the #w= workflow deep link now reacts to an in-page hashchange, not just a cold load. A visitor on /sandbox who clicks a #w= link in the nav (or the hash changes in-page) gets the workflow activated the same way a fresh page load does. One-line listener + a test asserting the wiring renders.

FIX #3: canonicalized the two divergent x-tick shims. The sandbox child harness had _set_xticks/_set_yticks and the gallery had a separate ax.xticks path — two copies of the same tick/label reconciliation rule, and the primes workflow step's 11-bucket/10-label mismatch (caught live in s30) was the first symptom they had drifted. Now a single pure _canonical_ticks(ticks, labels) is the one source of truth: it's spliced into the child harness verbatim via inspect.getsource at import time (so child == parent, mechanically impossible to drift, with a test locking that invariant) and the gallery's _Plt.routes through the same function. A count mismatch degrades (truncates labels) instead of crashing. 11 hermetic tests.

DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH: gunicorn now runs with --timeout 60 (systemd unit), so the worker kill threshold is 3x the health budget instead of 1.5x — the bound is the primary fix, this just widens the margin so a genuinely stuck request can't take down a worker. Unit validated with systemd-analyze verify.
